title: Anthropic's Junior Tech Hires Fall From 27% to 9% as AI Agents Outwork Staff
excerpt: The Claude maker's own employment report shows junior staff shrinking from 21% to 14% of its technical departments since early 2025, while AI agents logged six times as many hours as employees by August.
body:
• Junior technical hires at Anthropic fell from 27% to 9% of technical intakes, and junior staff slipped from 21% to 14% of technical departments since early 2025, the company's own report says.
  • By August 2026, AI agents directed by employees were working six times as many hours as their human handlers; code commits per engineer rose to five times their level of six months earlier.
  • Around a third of machine-learning managers and a fifth of software-engineering managers said they were hiring less because of AI. This is a falling share, not a freeze: Anthropic has tripled in size in a year and technical hiring still grew in absolute terms.
  • For early-career engineers, the hiring bar has moved: managers now weight autonomy, judgment and skill at directing AI tools — references to a candidate's AI track record in technical assessments roughly tripled between 2024 and 2026.

Anthropic, the company behind Claude, has published the clearest evidence yet that AI is eating the bottom rung of the tech career ladder — starting with its own. In a report titled "How Employment Is Changing at Anthropic," released on October 16, the Anthropic Institute found that the share of junior-level employees in its technical departments slipped from 21% to 14% since early 2025, while the proportion of junior technical hires fell from 27% to 9%. Postings for junior roles, the authors note, have fallen particularly sharply since December 2025.

The report, by Nathan Wilmers of MIT Sloan, Atlassian's Regina Catipon and Anthropic economists Maxim Massenkoff and Peter McCrory, draws on the company's internal employment, hiring and productivity records alongside interviews with 17 employees. Its findings were reported by NDTV and Mint. The figures are Anthropic's own and have not been independently verified.

Agents doing the junior work

The mechanism is direct. Teams that relied most on Claude found it could increasingly take over writing code and finding bugs — the tasks that traditionally trained junior engineers. By August, interactive AI agents directed by employees were working six times as many hours as the employees directing them, and combined agent hours had passed human hours for the first time in March. Code commits per engineer are running at about five times their level of six months earlier, though the authors caution that more code does not necessarily mean better code. One engineer described the new reality as facing "an army of Claudes, with every one asking for my attention." By April, engineering and research teams had deprioritised lower-level technical hiring.

"Employment protections for incumbents will not benefit those not hired to begin with."

— How Employment Is Changing at Anthropic, Anthropic Institute

What hiring managers want now

As routine execution is automated, the criteria for the humans who remain are shifting. Hiring managers now stress autonomy and judgment over narrow technical expertise, and increasingly score whether candidates use AI effectively. In 2024, managers noted a candidate's track record on AI tooling in about 5% of assessments for technical roles; by 2026 that rate had tripled for technical roles and quadrupled for non-technical roles. The composition of the company is changing with it: technical departments' share of total employment fell from 61% to 56% as sales, finance and recruiting grew faster.

Why it matters beyond one company

Anthropic argues it may be a leading indicator: it adopts AI faster than most employers, so its hiring mix could preview the wider economy's. For Indian graduates and early-career engineers targeting US tech roles, the signal is concrete — the portfolio that gets an interview is shifting from coursework and narrow coding drills toward demonstrated judgment in directing AI systems on real projects. The authors are frank about the policy gap: Anthropic has built an internal early-warning system to flag jobs at risk and is moving staff internally — employees with at least a year at the company were 50% more likely to switch departments each month in 2026 than in 2025 — but they concede none of this "directly addresses the slowdown in junior hires" and call on governments for retraining and income support. They also caution that Anthropic's explosive growth over the same period lifted output in ways that make its experience hard to replicate across the economy.

What to watch

The test is whether other large employers publish the same pattern. If junior postings keep falling while overall headcount grows, the industry's problem becomes structural: senior engineers are made, not hired, and a pipeline that stops taking in juniors eventually runs out of them.
